chunks: And with the first chain of narration from Ali ibn Mahziyar, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Abu Mu'adh al-Suddi, from Abu Arakah who said:

I prayed behind the Commander of the Believers, Ali ibn Abi Talib, blessings of Allah upon him, the dawn prayer in this mosque of yours. Then he turned to his right and there was gloom upon him. He remained until the sun rose upon the wall of this mosque of yours to the height of a spear, and it was not as it is today.

Then he turned to the people and said: Verily, by Allah, the companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family, used to endure this night, alternating between their foreheads and their knees, as if the roar of the Fire was in their ears. And when morning came, they were dust-covered and pale, with marks between their eyes resembling the knees of goats. And when Allah the Most High was mentioned, they swayed just as trees sway on a windy day, and tears flowed from their eyes until their clothes became wet.

He said: Then he stood up saying: By Allah, it is as if the people have spent the night heedlessly. Thereafter he was never seen cheerful until the affair of Ibn Muljam — may Allah curse him — took place.

key_terms.رُكَبِ الْمَعْزَى: Knees of goats; a metaphor for the prayer calluses (thafinaat) formed on their foreheads from prostration
key_terms.زَفِيرَ النَّارِ: The roaring/blazing of Hellfire; their spiritual state was as if they could hear its sound
key_terms.مَادُوا: To sway or tremble; describing their physical reaction of awe when Allah was mentioned
key_terms.مُفْتَرًّا: Cheerful, showing a broad smile; indicating Ali's perpetual sorrow after this sermon
key_terms.يُرَاوِحُونَ: To alternate between two positions; specifically prostration and standing in prayer
key_terms.يُكَابِدُونَ: To endure hardship; here referring to the physical and spiritual struggle of night worship

ai.seo_question: What did Imam Ali say about the companions of the Prophet and their night prayers?
ai.summary: Abu Arakah narrates that after leading the dawn prayer in the mosque of Kufa, Imam Ali (as) sat in deep gloom until sunrise. He then delivered a moving exhortation comparing the present community's laxity with the devotion of the Prophet's companions, who spent their nights in such intense prayer that they emerged dust-covered, pale, and calloused. After this sermon, Ali (as) was never again seen in a cheerful state until his assassination by Ibn Muljam. This narration reflects the Imam's grief over the spiritual decline of his community and serves as a reminder of the worship standards set by the earliest believers.
